sentences.text: To support his first stand regarding measurement, he has contended that, in fact, the total area of acquired land, i.e. House No. 22, situated at Padalsare, Tq. Amalner, Dist. Jalgaon, though, was 61.90 sq. mtr., but it was shown as 40.20 sq mtr.

He submitted that the said land was subjected to acquisition and the notification was issued under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, (published on 20th April 2006), for the Minor Tapi Project, Hatnur.

The notice was published in the gazette on 10 th April 2007, and on 26th September 2008, an award under section 11 the Land acquisition Act ,
was passed.

The Special Land Acquisition Officer has awarded Rs. 300 per sq. mtr., and therefore,
he had preferred reference under Section 18 before the Special Land Acquisition Officer, who then forwarded it.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant admitted that when reference was made, there was no issue regarding the size of the land, as in the original proceedings, the area acquired was shown as 31.20 sq. mtr. for construction, 9 sq. mtr. was for open space.

Thus, the total area acquired was 31.20 sq.
mtr. when claimant realised that in fact the acquired area was 61.90 sq. mtr., an application below Exhibit 16 was preferred for amendment in the reference.

In the said application dated 12th January 2025, a request was made that he 972-FA-3870-19.odt be permitted to carry out the amendment to show that the total acquired land was in fact 61.9 sq. mtr.
5.

According to him, the said application was allowed by the reference Court vide order dated 26 th March 2015 and accordingly, he carried out the necessary amendment.
6.

To prove his contention that less area was acquired, he examined CW 1 / Mahesh, who, on the date of deposition, was working on the post of Deputy Superintendent of Land Records, Amalner,
and has stated that on 27 th August 2014, the surveyor/measurer - Jadhav, measured the land in his presence.
CW 1 was then shown the list below, Exhibit 21, more particularly Sr. No. 2, which was the letter dated 25 th July 2024, on which the measurement was based.
The said latter was proved below Exhibit 29.
CW 1 deposed that in accordance with the letter, he visited this spot, carried out the measurement and prepared the measurement map, which bears the signature of CW 1.
He also identified the signature of the Clerk and the Sheristedar on the site map.
The said map is shown below as Exhibit 30.
In his examination- in-chief, he has categorically stated that during the measurement, he found that earlier measurements showed the land to be less.
According to the earlier measurement, the area was 40.02 sq. mtr., whereas, as per the measurement carried out by CW 1, the area was 61.875 sq. mtr.

He further deposed that he 972-FA-3870-19.odt had issued a notice to all concerned on 12 th August, 2014, regarding the carrying out of the measurement, and had proved the same below Exhibit 31.
7.
Learned counsel for the appellant then submitted that the cross- examination of this witness, if perused, nothing has been brought on record except giving a suggestion.
Further, this witness, in cross-examination, has stated that the measurement was carried out in 1999, which was a joint measurement and was correct.
But he clarified that the area was incorrect.

According to him, the reference Court should not have ignored the said piece of evidence, but the reference Court disregarded the evidence of this witness on the ground that he is not the author of the map in question.
He then contended that the said findings are not supported by evidence, as the testimony of CW 2 speaks otherwise.

Mr Patil, learned counsel for the acquiring body, submitted that the grounds regarding measurement are a fragile grounds and had there been a smaller area, at the stage of award itself,
the claimant would have raised an objection.

He has submitted that the witness examined, i.e. CW 2,
should not have believed upon, and the map is also liable to be discarded.
He further contended that there was nothing to disbelieve the measurement carried out at first, i.e., in the year 1999.
. So far as the issue of measurement is concerned, I have gone through the record of the case, and I have also given thoughtful consideration to the arguments advanced by the respective parties.

The record of the case would reveal that, since the claimant was not satisfied with the measurement, he preferred an application for amendment before the reference Court, requesting that the reference be amended to show the actual area as 61.9 sq. mtr.
The said amendment application was allowed by speaking order, and the respective counsels do not dispute that the order was not taken exception to in any proceeding.
Thus, the fact remains that the order allowing the amendment was not challenged by the acquiring body and has become final.
10. It is a well-settled principle of law that just because an amendment application is allowed, it does not mean that the contents of it is also proved.

In the present case, it was CW 1 who entered the witness box on behalf of the claimant and deposed that he worked at the office of the Superintendent of Land Records and supervised the measurement carried out by Mr Jadhav.
Even the measurement map was prepared, revealing that the acquired land was 61.9 sq. mtr.

This witness has categorically stated that he prepared the map, and further stated that in the earlier measurement, the area found was 40.02 sq. mtr., and in the measurement carried out by him, the area was 61.875 sq. mtr.
Before carrying out the measurement, notices were also issued to the interested persons, which were proved and brought on record.

. In the aforesaid background, it can be said that the due procedure was followed regarding bringing the factual aspect of measurement on record, as well as the evidence to prove that in the first measurement, a smaller area was shown.
Cross -
examination of this witness, which is not more than four sentences, would reveal that no attempt was made to seriously challenge the testimony of this witness.
The findings of the reference Court that CW 1 has not prepared the map are thus incorrect.

I thus held that the area of land acquired was 61.875 sq. mtr.
12.
This takes me to another limb of the argument advanced by learned counsel for the appellant regarding the valuation of the property.
Learned counsel for the appellant has submitted that the land acquisition officer has awarded a meagre sum of Rs 300/- per sq. mtr., and therefore, a reference was moved.

To prove the valuation of the house property, an expert witness, i.e., CW 2,
was examined.
According to Mr. Shaikh, the testimony of CW 2 was based upon the valuation report, which he had submitted, which was duly proved by this witness below Exhibit 42.

Inviting my attention to the findings given by the reference Court, Mr. Shaikh contended that the Court,
without there being any material, has concluded that the rate of depreciation given by the expert is Padmakar Ratan Patil vs Special Land Acquisition Officer (2) ... on 25 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167873200/
3 not proper.

sentences.text: The Court then suggested depreciation at 25%, though CW 2 had suggested 7% to 8%.
Mr. Shaikh then contended that there was absolutely no reason or material available before the reference 972-FA-3870-19.odt Court to decide the rate of depreciation, that too at 25%.
According to Mr. Shaikh, if the acquiring body wishes to challenge the expert evidence, cross- examination was the proper weapon that could have been used, but it was not.

13. Mr. Shaikh then invited my attention to the law laid down by this court in First Appeal No. 1293 of 2019, decided on 03rd May 2023, Namdeo and Ors. Vs. State of Maharashtra , decided by the Nagpur Bench of this High Court, more particularly the following paragraphs - "06] As it has been held by the Apex Court in Special Land Acquisition Officer and Another v. Sidappa Omanna Tumari and Others reported in 1995 Supp (2) SCC 168,
the Courts can act on an expert witness in determining the value of the land or structure.

entities.text: Namdeo and Ors. Vs. State of Maharashtra

sentences.text:
Nevertheless, because such expert witnesses are engaged by the Claimant,
the Court is required to be cautious while granting the report and evidence in support thereof.
The Apex Court has held that the valuation report is of no assistance if it is not based on factual data or material that is proved to be genuine and reliable.

Therefore, when a report of an expert is produced before the Court, the Court may choose to act upon such report, if the data or the material based on which such report is produced before the Court and the authenticity of the same is made good, and the method of valuation adopted therein is correct."
The aforesaid observations would reveal that the Court will have to see whether the valuation report is based on factual data or material and has been proved to be genuine and reliable.
Considering that the valuation report covers every aspect, it can be relied upon.
972-FA-3870-19.odt 14. Per contra, Mr. Patil, learned counsel for the acquiring body, has contended that according to the valuation report, the age of the property and the life was men and

Considering the aforesaid aspect,
the reference Court has rightly stated that 25% depreciation is just and proper.
He submitted that the reliance placed upon in the valuation report, more particularly Exhibits 51 to 53, was not correct.
He submitted that Exhibits 51 to 53, sale instances, though they were from an adjoining village, were at a far distance.
He then submitted that what is required to be granted is just compensation.
It should not be meagre, nor inflated.

He, therefore, contended that there is absolutely no material and, therefore, the appeal is liable to be dismissed.
15.
The issue of valuation is required to be appreciated in the background of evidence produced by the respective parties.
It is undisputed that rebuttal evidence is not produced by the acquiring body.
What remains is the testimony of the expert, i.e., CW 2, and the claimant/Padmakar, CW 3, below Exhibit 32.
The claimant, in his evidence on affidavit below Exhibit 32, has stated that the foundation of the house was of limestone, with brick and cement construction.
There were doors and windows.

The claimant deposed that he had requested Mr. Dinesh, the Expert Valuer, to visit the house on 23rd June 2006, who, after inspecting the property, prepared the panchnama and put Padmakar Ratan Patil vs Special Land Acquisition Officer (2) ... on 25 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167873200/
4 his signature, as well as the signature of the sarpanch of the village and members of the gram panchayat, as the panch witnesses.

sentences.text: 16. If cross-examination of this witness is perused, it would be crystal clear that except giving suggestion, nothing has been brought on record.
Needless to mention that the suggestion has no value in the eyes of the law if denied.
17. CW 2 was Dinesh Mutha, Expert Valuer witness, who was examined by the Claimant below Exhibit 34.
He had filed his evidence on affidavit and stated that he had 22 years of experience and was appointed as a valuer under the Wealth Tax Act, Income-tax Act, and Gift Tax Act.

He also stated that he is on the panel of valuers for various nationalised, cooperative, and scheduled banks,
and is a government-recognised valuer with a specific registration number.

18. CW 2 then contended that on 23rd June 2006, he visited the acquired property, carried out inspection and measurement, observed the geographical area, prepared the panchnama and valuation report by taking the signatures of the panchas and the claimant.
He further submitted that, for 972-FA-3870-19.odt determining the rate of depreciation, he adopted the district schedule rate.
He proved the valuation report below Exhibit 42, which is a detailed report dated 24th June 2006.
In the said report, the date on which valuation was conducted, the purpose of the valuation, a brief description of the property, technical details, the building's life and age, etc., were provided.

Further, a separate report under the heading 'Valuation Approach' is provided, in which the number of properties stated above was taken into consideration, and the rate of Rs. 1494/- per sq.mtr. was given as the property's valuation.

So far as deduction is concerned, those were also duly made,
except depreciation.
19. The cross-examination of this witness would reveal that, though every attempt was made to challenge his testimony, nothing was brought on record.

Just because the valuer had not brought the title document or relevant document about the property at the time of deposition, his evidence cannot be ignored, in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case.

As already stated, the valuation report though proved, but the fact remains that in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court in case of Namdeo (supra), so also Special Land Acquisition Officer and Anr. Vs.
Sidappa Omanna Tumari reported in 1995 Supp (2) SCC 168, the Court may choose to act upon the report if the data or material based on such material is produced before the Court.

Sidappa Omanna Tumari reported in 1995 Supp (2) SCC 168
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Needless to mention, the report cannot be held to be binding and will have to be seen whether it inspires confidence or not.
972-FA-3870-19.odt 20.
In the report, life of the building is stated to be of 70 years and age of building is 30 years.

Thus,
it can be seen that practical approach will have to be adopted for determining question of depreciation.

Neither the depreciation awarded by the valuer @ 7% to 8% is right nor the rate of Padmakar Ratan Patil vs Special Land Acquisition Officer (2) ... on 25 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167873200/

sentences.text: 5 25% arrived at by the reference Court needs to be awarded.

Considering the age and life of building,
it would be just and proper to calculate depreciation @ 15%.

21. Thus, as far as the aspect of depreciation is concerned, the reference Court has given 25% of depreciation and consequently deducted amount of Rs.1,61,719/-, which is clear from paragraph no.10 of the award passed by the reference Court.
As this Court has calculated the rate of depreciation at 15%, same would come to Rs.97,031/-.
Thus, only modification which is required is regarding deduction of amount of depreciation.
The amount which will now have to be deducted would be Rs.97,031/- as 15% depreciation.
Rest part of the calculation need not be disturbed.
22. In that view of the matter, I conclude that the valuer has rightly proved the valuation of the property but depreciation was not properly calculated by him.
Even the reference Court erred to conclude that depreciation @ 25% is required to be granted.
. The question of grant of interest is also required to be gone into.

At this stage, both parties have not disputed the law laid down by this Court in State of Maharashtra Vs. Kailash Shiva Rangari,
reported in 2016 AIR (Bom.) 141, has contended that the rate of interest be directed to be paid in accordance with the said judgment.
24.

entities.text:
State of Maharashtra Vs. Kailash Shiva Rangari,
reported in 2016 AIR (Bom.) 141
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In that view of the matter, I pass the following order :-
ORDER (I) First appeal is partly allowed.

(II) The claimant shall be entitled to the interest as per the law laid down by this Court in Kailash Shiva Rangari (Supra).
(III) The depreciation calculated by the reference Court @ 25% and thereby deducting an amount of Rs.1,61,719/- is modified.
The depreciation is now will have to be calculated @ 15% and amount will have to be deducted accordingly.
Rest of the award passed by the Reference Court is maintained.
(IV) Award be drawn accordingly.
(V) The deficit Court fee, if any, shall be paid by the claimant.
( RAJNISH R. VYAS, J. )
